phase1.explanation:
Byte streams treat everything as raw numbers — which is exactly wrong for text. A file of English text and a file of Japanese text are both "just bytes" as far as FileInputStream is concerned, and turning those bytes back into readable characters correctly depends on knowing the encoding they were written in. [[term:Character streams]] handle that translation for you.

[[term:FileReader]] and [[term:FileWriter]] are the character-stream equivalents of FileInputStream/FileOutputStream — but instead of raw bytes, they work in actual characters (and Strings), decoding and encoding as needed behind the scenes. write(text) takes a whole String directly; you don't manually convert it to bytes first.

[[key:FileWriter has two constructor modes worth knowing]]: new FileWriter("file.txt") overwrites the file completely, while new FileWriter("file.txt", true) — that second true — appends to whatever's already there instead of replacing it. Easy to forget, and the difference between losing a file's old content and keeping it.

[[warn:one genuinely surprising trap]]: FileWriter.write(int) doesn't write the NUMBER as text — it writes the CHARACTER that number represents. fw.write(65) writes the letter 'A' (ASCII 65), not the two characters "65". If you actually want the digits, convert first: fw.write(String.valueOf(65));.

Same rule as byte streams: [[key:always close what you open]] — character streams need it just as much, and try-with-resources handles it exactly the same way here too.
phase1.openingDialogue: Character streams — text handling made easy~ 📝

phase2.errorMessage: (No error — but the output is WRONG! File contains "AB", not "6566")
phase2.explanation:
fw.write(65) doesn't write the text "65" — it writes the CHARACTER whose ASCII code is 65, which happens to be the letter 'A'. Same story for write(66) → 'B'. The file ends up containing "AB", not "6566" — and there's no error anywhere, because this is completely legal, correctly-typed code that just doesn't do what you probably meant.

[[warn:this is the single most common surprise with character-stream write(int)]] — it's easy to assume write() always treats its argument as text, and it doesn't, when the argument is a raw int.

[[key:to actually write a number as readable text, convert it to a String first]]: fw.write(String.valueOf(65)); or fw.write(Integer.toString(65));, either one writes "65" as two literal digit characters.
phase2.openingDialogue: Watch what happens when a number gets written as a character~

A) The text "65"
B) The character 'A'
C) A compile error
D) The byte value 65 in binary form

phase4.selfChallenge:
Write a program that:
1. Creates a text file called "notes.txt"
2. Writes three lines of text using FileWriter
3. Reads the file back using FileReader
4. Prints the content line by line

Use try-with-resources for both operations.

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Fun fact]]: character encoding issues like this were common enough in real software that they eventually got a name — mojibake, borrowed from Japanese, describing the garbled text you get when a program reads bytes using the wrong encoding. Character streams exist specifically to spare you from having to think about encoding manually every time you touch a text file.
phase5.openingDialogue: One more thought before you go~
